body: Estonian licence plates are long and white, with the standard blue European strip on the left.

Estonian bollards have a round, baton-like shape with a rectangular reflector on the front and two circular ones on the back. The reflectors can be white or orange, and this design is distinct from bollards in Latvia and Lithuania.
Estonia has the least consistent utility poles of the Baltics, but round wooden poles are the most common type, sometimes featuring diagonal supports.
You can also find square concrete poles, often with diagonal supports, which are similar to those in Lithuania.
Trident poletops, with one insulator on top and two to the side, are somewhat common in Estonia.
Most wooden poles have a small metal cap on top, a feature shared with Nordic countries and occasionally Latvia.
Outer road lines in Estonia sometimes consist of short dashes. This feature is also found in Lithuania and Sweden.
Estonia uses red chevrons with white arrows, distinguishing it from Latvia and Lithuania which use the opposite color scheme. Russia and Ukraine use the same chevrons as Estonia.
While all Baltic countries use a blue kilometre marker, in Estonia it is positioned perpendicular to the road and has numbers on both sides.
Estonian warning and speed signs have a thin red border with no white outline, extending all the way to the edge of the sign.
Estonia uses normal A-type guardrails with no reflectors, which helps distinguish it from Latvia and Lithuania.

Estonian pedestrian signs have 3 stripes and feature a detailed pedestrian shape with shoes and an attached head. This helps distinguish them from less detailed Lithuanian signs and Latvian signs which have 5 stripes.
The Estonian bus stop sign features a bus with four windows. This distinguishes it from the Latvian sign (five windows), but not the Lithuanian one.
Blue and white signpost wrappings are very common in Estonia, but they can also be found in Finland and Sweden.
The Estonian language is Finnic, related to Finnish, and uses unique letters like Ä, Ö, Ü, and Õ. This makes it look very different from Latvian and Lithuanian.
The Estonian words for street and road are 'tänav' and 'tee', which are unique to the language. 'Tänav' is often abbreviated as 'tn'.
Oval-shaped blue house numbers are fairly common in Estonia. While not typical in other Baltic countries, they can also be found in Russia.
Estonian architecture often features a mix of wood and white brick, with steep corrugated metal roofs. Wooden buildings are more common in Estonia than in the other Baltic states.

Estonian directional signs are blue with a white outline and a simple arrow icon inside. This differs from Finnish signs where the arrow is part of the border, and Latvian signs which have a more stylized arrow.
Generation 3 coverage in Estonia often has a slight green tint, known as 'green blur'. This feature is generally absent in Latvia and Lithuania but can be seen in Sweden.
Estonia has more extensive Generation 3 coverage on very rural roads compared to Latvia and Lithuania. This can be a helpful, though not always reliable, clue in ambiguous situations.
Estonia is mostly flat, but recognizable hilly areas can be found in the southeast and in southern Lääne-Viru County.
Due to a large Russian minority, especially in Ida-Viru County, you may see bilingual signs with Russian Cyrillic text alongside Estonian, particularly around Narva.
The Old Town of Tallinn is a well-preserved historic area with medieval and Renaissance buildings, giving it a distinct Central European look compared to the rest of Estonia.
The island of Kihnu has distinctive Generation 4 coverage taken in late autumn with a moody, dark sky close to sunset.
